claim: The eukaryotic nucleosome comprises a protein octamer that wraps approximately 147 bp of DNA.
source: The eukaryotic nucleosome is the fundamental unit of chromatin, comprising a protein octamer that wraps ∼147 bp of DNA and has essential roles in DNA compaction, replication and gene expression.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about eukaryotic nucleosome structure.

claim: Eukaryotic nucleosomes have essential roles in DNA compaction, replication and gene expression.
source: The eukaryotic nucleosome is the fundamental unit of chromatin, comprising a protein octamer that wraps ∼147 bp of DNA and has essential roles in DNA compaction, replication and gene expression.
evidence: This represents established scientific consensus about nucleosome function.

claim: Select archaea have histone protein homologs that assemble into tetrameric nucleosomes.
source: Nucleosomes and chromatin have historically been considered to be unique to eukaryotes, yet studies of select archaea have identified homologs of histone proteins that assemble into tetrameric nucleosomes.
evidence: This is supported by prior studies referenced in the manuscript.

claim: This study reports the first archaeal genome-wide nucleosome occupancy map.
source: Here we report the first archaeal genome-wide nucleosome occupancy map, as observed in the halophile Haloferax volcanii.
evidence: This is a primary finding directly stated by the authors.

claim: Archaeal transcripts possess nucleosome-depleted regions at transcriptional start sites.
source: We found that archaeal transcripts possess hallmarks of eukaryotic chromatin structure: nucleosome-depleted regions at transcriptional start sites and conserved −1 and +1 promoter nucleosomes.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the nucleosome occupancy and transcriptome data presented.

claim: Archaeal transcripts possess conserved −1 and +1 promoter nucleosomes.
source: We found that archaeal transcripts possess hallmarks of eukaryotic chromatin structure: nucleosome-depleted regions at transcriptional start sites and conserved −1 and +1 promoter nucleosomes.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the nucleosome occupancy data.

claim: Histones and chromatin architecture evolved before the divergence of Archaea and Eukarya.
source: Our observations demonstrate that histones and chromatin architecture evolved before the divergence of Archaea and Eukarya, suggesting that the fundamental role of chromatin in the regulation of gene expression is ancient.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the conservation of chromatin features observed in the data.

claim: The fundamental role of chromatin in the regulation of gene expression is ancient.
source: Our observations demonstrate that histones and chromatin architecture evolved before the divergence of Archaea and Eukarya, suggesting that the fundamental role of chromatin in the regulation of gene expression is ancient.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation of chromatin architecture between archaea and eukaryotes.

claim: Archaeal nucleosome core particles protect approximately 60 bp of DNA.
source: Archaeal nucleosome core particles protect ∼60 bp of DNA, approximately half that of eukaryotic nucleosomes, as demonstrated by the landmark work of Pereira et al. (1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pereira et al. (1997).

claim: Archaeal nucleosomes protect approximately half the DNA length of eukaryotic nucleosomes.
source: Archaeal nucleosome core particles protect ∼60 bp of DNA, approximately half that of eukaryotic nucleosomes, as demonstrated by the landmark work of Pereira et al. (1997).
evidence: This is based on comparison of known values for archaeal (~60 bp) and eukaryotic (~147 bp) nucleosomes.

claim: Eukaryotic nucleosomes are octamers composed of heterodimers of histones H2A, H2B, H3 and H4.
source: Comparing both eukaryotic and archaeal nucleosomes, the former is an octamer composed of heterodimers of histones H2A, H2B, H3 and H4 whereas the latter histones assemble from homologs of H3 and H4 proteins (Pereira and Reeve, 1998; Talbert and Henikoff, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Archaeal histones assemble from homologs of H3 and H4 proteins.
source: Comparing both eukaryotic and archaeal nucleosomes, the former is an octamer composed of heterodimers of histones H2A, H2B, H3 and H4 whereas the latter histones assemble from homologs of H3 and H4 proteins (Pereira and Reeve, 1998; Talbert and Henikoff, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Archaeal histones can form both homodimers and heterodimers, as well as homotetramers.
source: Archaeal histones can form both homodimers and heterodimers, as well as homotetramers, whereas eukaryotic histones contain hydrophobic dimerization surfaces that restrict assembly of the octamer from H2A-H2B and H3-H4 heterodimers (Sandman and Reeve, 2006; Talbert and Henikoff, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Eukaryotic histones contain hydrophobic dimerization surfaces that restrict assembly of the octamer from H2A-H2B and H3-H4 heterodimers.
source: Archaeal histones can form both homodimers and heterodimers, as well as homotetramers, whereas eukaryotic histones contain hydrophobic dimerization surfaces that restrict assembly of the octamer from H2A-H2B and H3-H4 heterodimers (Sandman and Reeve, 2006; Talbert and Henikoff, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Haloferax volcanii is a halophilic archaeon and a member of the phylum euryarchaeota.
source: We constructed a nucleosome occupancy map of the halophilic archaeon Haloferax volcanii, a member of the phylum euryarchaeota, originally discovered in the highly saline sediment of the Dead Sea (Mullakhanbhai and Larsen, 1975).
evidence: This is established taxonomic information supported by citation.

claim: Haloferax volcanii was originally discovered in the highly saline sediment of the Dead Sea.
source: We constructed a nucleosome occupancy map of the halophilic archaeon Haloferax volcanii, a member of the phylum euryarchaeota, originally discovered in the highly saline sediment of the Dead Sea (Mullakhanbhai and Larsen, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the original discovery.

claim: The genome of Hfx. volcanii has an average GC content of 65%.
source: The genome of Hfx. volcanii has an average GC content of 65% and a total genome length of 4 Mb (Hartman et al., 2010) composed of five circular genetic elements: a 2.8 Mb main chromosome, three smaller chromosomes pHV1, pHV3 and pHV4 and the plasmid pHV2.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the genome publication.

claim: The genome of Hfx. volcanii has a total genome length of 4 Mb.
source: The genome of Hfx. volcanii has an average GC content of 65% and a total genome length of 4 Mb (Hartman et al., 2010) composed of five circular genetic elements: a 2.8 Mb main chromosome, three smaller chromosomes pHV1, pHV3 and pHV4 and the plasmid pHV2.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the genome publication.

claim: The Hfx. volcanii genome is composed of five circular genetic elements: a 2.8 Mb main chromosome, three smaller chromosomes pHV1, pHV3 and pHV4 and the plasmid pHV2.
source: The genome of Hfx. volcanii has an average GC content of 65% and a total genome length of 4 Mb (Hartman et al., 2010) composed of five circular genetic elements: a 2.8 Mb main chromosome, three smaller chromosomes pHV1, pHV3 and pHV4 and the plasmid pHV2.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the genome publication.

claim: Hfx. volcanii is highly polyploid with approximately 15 genome copies during exponential growth.
source: It is highly polyploid with ∼15 genome copies during exponential growth and ∼10 during stationary phase (Breuert et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Hfx. volcanii has approximately 10 genome copies during stationary phase.
source: It is highly polyploid with ∼15 genome copies during exponential growth and ∼10 during stationary phase (Breuert et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The histone protein of Hfx. volcanii is hstA (HVO_0520).
source: The histone protein of Hfx. volcanii, hstA (HVO_0520), has a domain architecture containing two distinct histone fold domains within the same peptide that heterodimerize similar to the Methanopyrus kandleri histone (HMk) (Geer et al., 2002; Talbert and Henikoff, 2010; Marchler-Bauer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by domain analysis and citations.

claim: The hstA protein has a domain architecture containing two distinct histone fold domains within the same peptide.
source: The histone protein of Hfx. volcanii, hstA (HVO_0520), has a domain architecture containing two distinct histone fold domains within the same peptide that heterodimerize similar to the Methanopyrus kandleri histone (HMk) (Geer et al., 2002; Talbert and Henikoff, 2010; Marchler-Bauer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by domain analysis and citations.

claim: The hstA histone fold domains heterodimerize similar to the Methanopyrus kandleri histone (HMk).
source: The histone protein of Hfx. volcanii, hstA (HVO_0520), has a domain architecture containing two distinct histone fold domains within the same peptide that heterodimerize similar to the Methanopyrus kandleri histone (HMk) (Geer et al., 2002; Talbert and Henikoff, 2010; Marchler-Bauer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Hfx. volcanii was cultured in rich media containing 2 M NaCl.
source: We cultured Hfx. volcanii in rich media containing 2 M NaCl (Mullakhanbhai and Larsen, 1975).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions used in the study.

claim: Mononucleosome-sized DNA fragments in Hfx. volcanii are 50-60 bp in length.
source: Mononucleosome-sized (50–60 bp) DNA fragments were gel purified and libraries were sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq2000 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data and Figure 1A showing the gel.

claim: The nucleosome occupancy data was significantly different than the control MNase digest of deproteinized 'naked' genomic DNA (r = 0.071).
source: The nucleosome occupancy data was significantly different than the control MNase digest of deproteinized 'naked' genomic DNA (r = 0.071), indicating that the nucleosome map is unaffected by any potential MNase sequence bias (Chung et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: The nucleosome map is unaffected by any potential MNase sequence bias.
source: The nucleosome occupancy data was significantly different than the control MNase digest of deproteinized 'naked' genomic DNA (r = 0.071), indicating that the nucleosome map is unaffected by any potential MNase sequence bias (Chung et al., 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the low correlation with naked DNA control.

claim: The mean peak-to-peak distance for the main chromosome was 68.5 bp in genic regions.
source: In the smoothed signal, the mean peak-to-peak distance for the main chromosome was 68.5 bp in genic regions and 76.1 bp in non-genic regions.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the nucleosome occupancy analysis.

claim: The mean peak-to-peak distance for the main chromosome was 76.1 bp in non-genic regions.
source: In the smoothed signal, the mean peak-to-peak distance for the main chromosome was 68.5 bp in genic regions and 76.1 bp in non-genic regions.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the nucleosome occupancy analysis.

claim: Genic regions were defined as the transcribed region plus 40 bp upstream of the 5′ end.
source: Genic regions were defined as the transcribed region plus 40 bp (the average promoter length based on Palmer and Daniels, 1995) upstream of the 5′ end.
evidence: This describes the operational definition used in the analysis, based on cited promoter length.

claim: The average promoter length in Hfx. volcanii is 40 bp.
source: Genic regions were defined as the transcribed region plus 40 bp (the average promoter length based on Palmer and Daniels, 1995) upstream of the 5′ end.
evidence: This is based on citation to Palmer and Daniels, 1995.

claim: Greater nucleosome density is observed in Hfx. volcanii vs all eukaryotes.
source: We observed a greater nucleosome density in Hfx. volcanii vs all eukaryotes likely due to the shorter length of DNA wrapped around the archaeal histone tetramer (Pereira et al., 1997).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the measured nucleosome density with known eukaryotic values.

claim: The greater nucleosome density in Hfx. volcanii is likely due to the shorter length of DNA wrapped around the archaeal histone tetramer.
source: We observed a greater nucleosome density in Hfx. volcanii vs all eukaryotes likely due to the shorter length of DNA wrapped around the archaeal histone tetramer (Pereira et al., 1997).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known structural differences between archaeal and eukaryotic nucleosomes.

claim: The Hfx. volcanii genome has 14.2 nucleosomes per kilobase.
source: Based on our data, the Hfx. volcanii genome has 14.2 nucleosomes per kilobase compared to 5.2 nucleosomes per kilobase in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the nucleosome occupancy data.

claim: Saccharomyces cerevisiae has 5.2 nucleosomes per kilobase.
source: Based on our data, the Hfx. volcanii genome has 14.2 nucleosomes per kilobase compared to 5.2 nucleosomes per kilobase in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
evidence: This is a comparison value, likely from prior knowledge or literature.

claim: The nucleosome map reveals a periodic pattern similar to that seen in all eukaryotes examined to date.
source: The resulting map reveals a periodic pattern similar to that seen in all eukaryotes examined to date; with protected regions appearing as peaks and linker regions as troughs.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the observed pattern with known eukaryotic patterns.

claim: Nucleosome midpoints in Hfx. volcanii were enriched with G/C nucleotides from 61.4% GC at the edge of the protected fragment to 74.6% GC at the midpoint (dyad).
source: Sequence analysis of the entire nucleosome map showed that nucleosome midpoints were enriched with G/C nucleotides from 61.4% GC at the edge of the protected fragment to 74.6% GC at the midpoint (dyad).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from sequence analysis of the nucleosome map.

claim: There is an increase of G/C nucleotides and a decrease in A/T nucleotides at the nucleosome midpoint in Hfx. volcanii.
source: We found an increase of G/C nucleotides and a decrease in A/T nucleotides at the midpoint, as described recently for human cell lines (Figure 1B,C) (Valouev et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1B,C and comparison with human cell lines.

claim: An increase of G/C nucleotides and a decrease in A/T nucleotides at the nucleosome midpoint has been described recently for human cell lines.
source: We found an increase of G/C nucleotides and a decrease in A/T nucleotides at the midpoint, as described recently for human cell lines (Figure 1B,C) (Valouev et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Valouev et al., 2011.

claim: No periodicity in dinucleotide frequency relative to the nucleosome midpoint was observed in Hfx. volcanii.
source: In contrast to previous studies in eukaryotes, we did not observe a periodicity in dinucleotide frequency relative to the nucleosome midpoint (Satchwell et al., 1986; Bailey et al., 2000; Albert et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a negative result from the sequence analysis, contrasting with eukaryotic studies.

claim: Periodicity in dinucleotide frequency relative to the nucleosome midpoint has been observed in previous studies in eukaryotes.
source: In contrast to previous studies in eukaryotes, we did not observe a periodicity in dinucleotide frequency relative to the nucleosome midpoint (Satchwell et al., 1986; Bailey et al., 2000; Albert et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior eukaryotic studies.

claim: The existing genome annotation for Haloferax is derived almost exclusively from ORF predictions.
source: The existing genome annotation for Haloferax is derived almost exclusively from ORF predictions (Hartman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the genome annotation.

claim: Deep sequencing was used to create a high confidence transcriptome of the main chromosome of Hfx. volcanii.
source: To augment these predictions, we used deep sequencing to create a high confidence transcriptome of the main chromosome of Hfx. volcanii.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: The transcriptome map allowed definition of 5′UTR lengths, transcriptional start sites (TSSs) and transcriptional termination sites (TTSs).
source: This map allowed us to define both 5′UTR lengths, transcriptional start sites (TSSs) and transcriptional termination sites (TTSs).
evidence: This describes the information obtained from the transcriptome analysis.

claim: Duplex-specific nuclease (DSN) normalization was used to partially deplete repetitive RNA.
source: Total RNA was extracted from Hfx. volcanii cells, repetitive RNA was partially depleted via duplex-specific nuclease (DSN) normalization followed by RNA-seq (see 'Materials and methods') (Zhulidov et al., 2004).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used.

claim: The final set of transcripts were manually curated yielding 3059 transcriptional units in Hfx. volcanii.
source: The final set of transcripts were manually curated yielding 3059 transcriptional units in Hfx. volcanii, a number that is greater than observed previously in the comparable transcriptome of the sulfur-metabolizing archaeon Sulfolobus solfataricus (Wurtzel et al., 2010) but fewer than the 4073 predicted Hfx. volcanii genes.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the transcriptome analysis.

claim: The number of transcriptional units in Hfx. volcanii (3059) is greater than observed previously in the comparable transcriptome of Sulfolobus solfataricus.
source: The final set of transcripts were manually curated yielding 3059 transcriptional units in Hfx. volcanii, a number that is greater than observed previously in the comparable transcriptome of the sulfur-metabolizing archaeon Sulfolobus solfataricus (Wurtzel et al., 2010) but fewer than the 4073 predicted Hfx. volcanii genes.
evidence: This is a comparison with prior work supported by citation.

claim: The number of transcriptional units in Hfx. volcanii (3059) is fewer than the 4073 predicted Hfx. volcanii genes.
source: The final set of transcripts were manually curated yielding 3059 transcriptional units in Hfx. volcanii, a number that is greater than observed previously in the comparable transcriptome of the sulfur-metabolizing archaeon Sulfolobus solfataricus (Wurtzel et al., 2010) but fewer than the 4073 predicted Hfx. volcanii genes.
evidence: This is a comparison with the predicted gene count.

claim: 75% of the predicted transcripts were detectably expressed in the rich media conditions used in this study.
source: It is likely that in the rich media conditions used in this study, not all genes are expressed. Specifically 75% of the predicted transcripts were detectably expressed, and this fraction is consistent with observations obtained for yeast gene expression in rich media (David et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the transcriptome data.

claim: The fraction of expressed genes (75%) is consistent with observations obtained for yeast gene expression in rich media.
source: It is likely that in the rich media conditions used in this study, not all genes are expressed. Specifically 75% of the predicted transcripts were detectably expressed, and this fraction is consistent with observations obtained for yeast gene expression in rich media (David et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with cited yeast data.

claim: Thirty-two novel transcripts absent from the predicted sequence annotation were identified in the RNA-seq data.
source: Thirty-two novel transcripts (absent from the predicted sequence annotation) were identified in the RNA-seq data.
evidence: This is a result from the transcriptome analysis.

claim: Most of the 32 novel transcripts lack significant sequence homologs.
source: Most of these 32 transcripts lack significant sequence homologs, and several were classified as transposases with paralogs in Hfx. volcanii (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on homology analysis of the novel transcripts.

claim: Several of the 32 novel transcripts were classified as transposases with paralogs in Hfx. volcanii.
source: Most of these 32 transcripts lack significant sequence homologs, and several were classified as transposases with paralogs in Hfx. volcanii (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence classification and homology analysis.

claim: NTRANS_0004 was the most highly expressed gene in the transcriptome and was not previously annotated.
source: Notably, the gene that was most highly expressed in the transcriptome (NTRANS_0004) was not previously annotated and contains a putative N-Acyltransferase (NAT) superfamily domain.
evidence: This is a result from the transcriptome analysis.

claim: NTRANS_0004 contains a putative N-Acyltransferase (NAT) superfamily domain.
source: Notably, the gene that was most highly expressed in the transcriptome (NTRANS_0004) was not previously annotated and contains a putative N-Acyltransferase (NAT) superfamily domain.
evidence: This is based on domain analysis of the sequence.

claim: NTRANS_0004 appears to be restricted to the genomes of other halophilic archaea.
source: Homology searches revealed that this transcript appears to be restricted to the genomes of other halophilic archaea (Altschul et al., 1990).
evidence: This is based on homology searches.

claim: The architecture of the NTRANS_0004 domain is homologous to chain A of the well-characterized histone acetyltransferases Gcn5, Gna1, Hpa2 in S. cerevisiae.
source: The architecture of this domain is homologous to chain A of the well-characterized histone acetyltransferases Gcn5, Gna1, Hpa2 in S. cerevisiae, suggesting a possible role for this transcript in regulating transcription via histone acetylation (Marchler-Bauer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on domain architecture comparison.

claim: NTRANS_0004 may have a possible role in regulating transcription via histone acetylation.
source: The architecture of this domain is homologous to chain A of the well-characterized histone acetyltransferases Gcn5, Gna1, Hpa2 in S. cerevisiae, suggesting a possible role for this transcript in regulating transcription via histone acetylation (Marchler-Bauer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is speculation based on domain homology.

claim: Additional acyltransferases with a similar architecture have been implicated in bacteriophage-encoded DNA modifiers.
source: Additional acyltransferases with a similar architecture have been implicated in bacteriophage-encoded DNA modifiers as well as in cold and ethanol tolerance in yeast (Du and Takagi, 2007; Kaminska and Bujnicki, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Additional acyltransferases with a similar architecture have been implicated in cold and ethanol tolerance in yeast.
source: Additional acyltransferases with a similar architecture have been implicated in bacteriophage-encoded DNA modifiers as well as in cold and ethanol tolerance in yeast (Du and Takagi, 2007; Kaminska and Bujnicki, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Histone post-translational modifications have not been observed in archaeal histones.
source: Thus, while histone post-translational modifications have not been observed in archaeal histones (Forbes et al., 2004), our observation suggests that some rudimentary control over chromatin accessibility may occur via the action of ancient NAT family members.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Some rudimentary control over chromatin accessibility may occur via the action of ancient NAT family members.
source: Thus, while histone post-translational modifications have not been observed in archaeal histones (Forbes et al., 2004), our observation suggests that some rudimentary control over chromatin accessibility may occur via the action of ancient NAT family members.
evidence: This is speculation based on the identification of NAT domain-containing proteins.

claim: Acetyltransferase and deacetylase orthologs have been identified in Hfx. volcanii.
source: Furthermore acetyltransferase and deacetylase orthologs, which appear to have enzymatic activity based on their sensitivity to the histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor trichostatin A have been identified in Hfx. volcanii (Altman-Price and Mevarech, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Acetyltransferase and deacetylase orthologs in Hfx. volcanii appear to have enzymatic activity based on their sensitivity to the histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor trichostatin A.
source: Furthermore acetyltransferase and deacetylase orthologs, which appear to have enzymatic activity based on their sensitivity to the histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor trichostatin A have been identified in Hfx. volcanii (Altman-Price and Mevarech, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In eukaryotes, the TSS of the majority of expressed genes is characterized by a nucleosome-depleted region (NDR).
source: In eukaryotes, the TSS of the majority of expressed genes is characterized by a nucleosome-depleted region (NDR) (Jiang and Pugh, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about eukaryotic chromatin structure supported by citation.

claim: In eukaryotes, the NDR is flanked by the well-positioned −1 and the +1 nucleosomes.
source: This NDR is flanked by the well-positioned −1 and the +1 nucleosomes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about eukaryotic chromatin structure.

claim: NDRs and flanking nucleosomes direct RNA polymerase II to initiate transcription and influence the binding of promoter regulatory elements.
source: These regions direct RNA polymerase II to initiate transcription and influence the binding of promoter regulatory elements (Jiang and Pugh, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The stereotypical pattern of nucleosome depletion at promoters and well-ordered nucleosomes in gene bodies is found in all eukaryotes, including yeast, Drosophila, Arabidopsis and humans.
source: This stereotypical pattern of nucleosome depletion at promoters and well-ordered nucleosomes in gene bodies is found in all eukaryotes, including yeast, Drosophila, Arabidopsis and humans.
evidence: This is established knowledge about eukaryotic chromatin structure.

claim: The NDR and −1 and +1 nucleosomes are conserved in Hfx. volcanii.
source: Using the RNA-seq-derived transcripts for Hfx. volcanii, we computed the degree of aggregate nucleosome occupancy for the 2343 transcripts on the main chromosome, and found that the NDR and −1 and +1 nucleosomes are conserved in Hfx. volcanii (Figure 2) suggesting that the interplay between chromatin and transcription is conserved in archaeal promoters.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the nucleosome occupancy data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The interplay between chromatin and transcription is conserved in archaeal promoters.
source: Using the RNA-seq-derived transcripts for Hfx. volcanii, we computed the degree of aggregate nucleosome occupancy for the 2343 transcripts on the main chromosome, and found that the NDR and −1 and +1 nucleosomes are conserved in Hfx. volcanii (Figure 2) suggesting that the interplay between chromatin and transcription is conserved in archaeal promoters.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation of NDR and flanking nucleosomes.

claim: Differential nucleosome density was observed with profiles encompassing between four to six nucleosomes in a 400-bp DNA segment spanning 200 bp on each side of the TSS.
source: We generated nucleosome occupancy profiles for each transcript and clustered them hierarchically. Differential nucleosome density was observed with profiles encompassing between four to six nucleosomes in a 400-bp DNA segment spanning 200 bp on each side of the TSS (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a result from the hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: NDRs at TTSs are observed in Hfx. volcanii.
source: NDRs at TTSs are also observed, and similar to those found in eukaryotes (Lee et al., 2007) they are less prominent than promoter NDRs in Hfx. volcanii (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3.

claim: NDRs at TTSs in Hfx. volcanii are less prominent than promoter NDRs.
source: NDRs at TTSs are also observed, and similar to those found in eukaryotes (Lee et al., 2007) they are less prominent than promoter NDRs in Hfx. volcanii (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3.

claim: NDRs at TTSs in eukaryotes are less prominent than promoter NDRs.
source: NDRs at TTSs are also observed, and similar to those found in eukaryotes (Lee et al., 2007) they are less prominent than promoter NDRs in Hfx. volcanii (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Genome-wide nucleosome occupancy is conserved between archaea and eukaryotes.
source: Our study establishes that genome-wide nucleosome occupancy is conserved between archaea and eukaryotes (Figure 4).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study supported by the data.

claim: Nucleosomal protected fragments are shorter in archaea than in eukaryotes.
source: We further show that the nucleosomal protected fragments and NDRs are shorter in archaea than in eukaryotes.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the measured fragment sizes with known eukaryotic values.

claim: NDRs are shorter in archaea than in eukaryotes.
source: We further show that the nucleosomal protected fragments and NDRs are shorter in archaea than in eukaryotes.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the measured NDR sizes with known eukaryotic values.

claim: Hfx. volcanii likely resembles a deeply rooted ancestor that possessed eukaryotic genome architecture hallmarks such as histones.
source: Our findings are particularly noteworthy because Hfx. volcanii likely resembles a deeply rooted ancestor that possessed eukaryotic genome architecture hallmarks such as histones, as well as bacterial hallmarks such as the Shine-Dalgarno sequence (Sartorius-Neef and Pfeifer, 2004).
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic position and features of Hfx. volcanii.

claim: Hfx. volcanii possesses bacterial hallmarks such as the Shine-Dalgarno sequence.
source: Our findings are particularly noteworthy because Hfx. volcanii likely resembles a deeply rooted ancestor that possessed eukaryotic genome architecture hallmarks such as histones, as well as bacterial hallmarks such as the Shine-Dalgarno sequence (Sartorius-Neef and Pfeifer, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Archaeal histone tetramers likely resemble an ancestral state of chromatin.
source: Archaeal histone tetramers likely resemble an ancestral state of chromatin, as it has been observed that functional (H3-H4)2 tetramers can be formed in vitro from eukaryotic histones, and these tetramers are functional; they facilitate more rapid transcription in vitro compared to native histone octamers (Puerta et al., 1993).
evidence: This is an inference based on the ability of eukaryotic H3-H4 to form functional tetramers.

claim: Functional (H3-H4)2 tetramers can be formed in vitro from eukaryotic histones.
source: Archaeal histone tetramers likely resemble an ancestral state of chromatin, as it has been observed that functional (H3-H4)2 tetramers can be formed in vitro from eukaryotic histones, and these tetramers are functional; they facilitate more rapid transcription in vitro compared to native histone octamers (Puerta et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Eukaryotic (H3-H4)2 tetramers facilitate more rapid transcription in vitro compared to native histone octamers.
source: Archaeal histone tetramers likely resemble an ancestral state of chromatin, as it has been observed that functional (H3-H4)2 tetramers can be formed in vitro from eukaryotic histones, and these tetramers are functional; they facilitate more rapid transcription in vitro compared to native histone octamers (Puerta et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The observation that archaea contain (H3-H4)2 tetramers is consistent with the proposal that formation of the canonical eukaryotic nucleosome octamer begins with (H3-H4)2 tetramer assembly.
source: The observation that archaea contain (H3-H4)2 tetramers is consistent with the proposal that formation of the canonical eukaryotic nucleosome octamer begins with (H3-H4)2 tetramer assembly (Talbert and Henikoff, 2010).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the archaeal structure with eukaryotic assembly models.

claim: Archaeal chromatin is not required for genome compaction.
source: As well, owing to the small bacterial-sized archaeal genome, we suggest that archaeal chromatin is not required for genome compaction.
evidence: This is speculation based on the small genome size.

claim: Higher-order chromatin is a eukaryotic invention.
source: This leads us to postulate that higher-order chromatin (Sajan and Hawkins, 2012) is a eukaryotic invention and that archaeal chromatin is necessary but not sufficient for genome compaction.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings and comparison with eukaryotes.

claim: Archaeal chromatin is necessary but not sufficient for genome compaction.
source: This leads us to postulate that higher-order chromatin (Sajan and Hawkins, 2012) is a eukaryotic invention and that archaeal chromatin is necessary but not sufficient for genome compaction.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings.

claim: Approximately 60 bp and 120 bp mono- and di-nucleosomes were observed in MNase-digested Hfx. volcanii chromatin.
